techniques.name: Factor Analysis
techniques.description: Factor analysis looks for a small number of hidden factors that explain why a larger set of measured variables, such as a model's input features, tend to move together. Each variable is modelled as a weighted mix of the shared factors plus a part that is unique to it, including measurement error. The weights are called loadings, and they show which variables each factor is built from; for example, several credit-history features might all load on one 'repayment behaviour' factor. Unlike principal component analysis, which summarises as much of the total variation as it can, factor analysis models only the variation that variables share. Analysts usually rotate the factors afterwards, using varimax (factors stay uncorrelated) or oblimin (factors may correlate), so that each variable loads mainly on one factor and the factors are easier to name.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team finds that forty macroeconomic and credit-bureau inputs to a default-risk model are heavily correlated. Exploratory factor analysis groups them into four factors the team can name, such as growth, inflation, household debt and credit conditions, and the model is rebuilt on the factor scores so its drivers can be explained to the risk committee in four terms instead of forty.

A flood-forecasting team with sixty correlated gauge, soil-moisture and satellite inputs runs factor analysis on the training data to find a few underlying drivers, such as rainfall intensity, catchment wetness and river level. Forecast explanations are then reported per driver, which operators can relate to what they see on the ground.

limitations.description: The standard model is linear, with each variable a weighted sum of factors plus noise. Maximum-likelihood extraction also assumes roughly normal data, so skewed, binary or strongly non-linear variables can distort the loadings. Check distributions first, or choose an extraction method that does not require normality.

Factors are statistical summaries of correlation, not discovered causes. A factor labelled 'economic confidence' is the analyst's reading of which variables load together, and a different rotation or sample may support a different label.

Sensitive to the choice of number of factors and rotation method, which have no single correct answer and can change both which variables group together and how readable the factors are. Report the choices made and check that the structure is stable.
Requires a sample that is large relative to the number of variables. With small samples the loadings are unstable and change when a few cases are added or removed.

Describes the structure of the data fed into it, not how a trained model uses that data. Factors of a model's inputs say nothing about which factors the model relies on, unless the model is also built on or analysed with the factor scores.

resources.title: A CFA example – lavaan tutorial
Overview and confirmatory and exploratory factor analysis of AI literacy scale
resources.abstract: Comprehensive concepts of AI literacy (AIL) and valid measures are essential for research (e.g., intervention studies) and practice (e.g., personnel selection/development) alike. To date, several scales have been published, sharing standard features but differing in some aspects. We first aim to briefly overview instruments identified from unsystematic literature research in February 2023. We identified four scales and one collection of items. We describe the instruments and compare them. We identified common themes and overlaps in the instruments and developmental procedure. We also found differences regarding scale development procedures and latent dimensions. Following this literature research, we came to the conclusion that the literature on AI literacy measurement was fragmented, and little effort was undertaken to integrate different AI literacy conceptualizations. The second focus of this study is to test the factorial structures of existing AIL measurement instruments and identify latent dimensions of AIL across all instruments. We used robust maximum-likelihood confirmatory factor analysis to test factorial structures in a joint survey of all AIL items in an English-speaking online sample ( N =219). We found general support for all instruments' factorial structures with minor deviations from the original factorial structures for some of the instruments. In a second analysis step, to address the issue of fragmented research on AI literacy conceptualization and measurement, we used principal axis exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation to identify latent dimensions across all items. We found four correlated latent dimensions of AIL, which were mostly interpretable as the abilities to use and interact with AI, to design/program AI (incl. in-depth technical knowledge), to perform complex cognitive operations regarding AI (e.g., ethical considerations), and a common factor for the abilities to detect AI/differentiate between AI and humans and manage persuasive influences of AI (i.e., persuasion literacy). Our findings sort the multitude of AIL instruments and reveal four latent core dimensions of AIL. Thus, they contribute importantly to the conceptual understanding of AIL that has been fragmented so far. • We give an overview of AI literacy measures. • Their factorial structures were mostly confirmed. • PA EFA identified four correlated latent dimensions across all instruments.

sample_claims.text: The default-risk model's correlated inputs reduce to a small number of named factors that account for most of their shared variance, so its drivers can be explained at factor level.
The flood-forecasting inputs group into a few factors whose loadings domain experts recognise as physically meaningful drivers.
The number of factors retained, the extraction method and the rotation are documented, and the factor structure is stable when the analysis is repeated on a separate sample.

techniques.name: Principal Component Analysis
techniques.description: Principal component analysis (PCA) summarises a dataset that has many numeric features by finding a few new axes along which the data varies most. Each axis, called a principal component, is a weighted mix of the original features. The first axis follows the direction of greatest spread in the data, the second follows the greatest remaining spread at right angles to the first, and so on. Plotting the data on the first two or three axes gives a view of its structure, and the weights show which features move together.

example_use_cases.description: A retail analyst runs PCA on three dozen customer behaviour measures and finds that two components account for most of the variation. The weights show that one axis mixes spend and basket size and the other mixes visit frequency and recency, which gives the team a short list of dimensions to examine before building a segmentation model.

A team building a face verification system runs PCA on its training images and displays the leading components as images. If those components mainly capture lighting or background rather than face shape, the team knows the dataset's main variation reflects how the photos were taken, and can change what it collects.

A researcher auditing a word embedding takes the difference vectors for ten gendered word pairs, such as he and she, and runs PCA. The first component explains far more variance than the rest and far more than for random vectors, which suggests the embedding encodes gender mostly along one direction (Bolukbasi et al., 2016).

limitations.description: Each component mixes many original features, so it often has no clear real-world meaning, and the weights are hard to read when there are many features.
PCA captures only linear structure, so it can miss curved or clustered patterns in the data and interactions between features.

Results depend on feature scaling. PCA centres the data but does not rescale it, so a feature measured in large units can dominate the leading components. Standardise features first, or the components may reflect units and not structure.

PCA ranks directions by how much the data varies, not by how much they matter for an outcome. A high-variance component may be noise or irrelevant to a decision, and a low-variance one may carry the signal that separates classes, so leading components are not a guide to what a model needs.

Dropping components discards the variance they carry. Deciding how many to keep is a judgement call, for example a target share of variance explained, and it trades a simpler summary against lost detail.

resources.title: Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker? Debiasing Word Embeddings
resources.abstract: The blind application of machine learning runs the risk of amplifying biases present in data. Such a danger is facing us with word embedding, a popular framework to represent text data as vectors which has been used in many machine learning and natural language processing tasks. We show that even word embeddings trained on Google News articles exhibit female/male gender stereotypes to a disturbing extent. This raises concerns because their widespread use, as we describe, often tends to amplify these biases. Geometrically, gender bias is first shown to be captured by a direction in the word embedding. Second, gender neutral words are shown to be linearly separable from gender definition words in the word embedding. Using these properties, we provide a methodology for modifying an embedding to remove gender stereotypes, such as the association between between the words receptionist and female, while maintaining desired associations such as between the words queen and female. We define metrics to quantify both direct and indirect gender biases in embeddings, and develop algorithms to "debias" the embedding. Using crowd-worker evaluation as well as standard benchmarks, we empirically demonstrate that our algorithms significantly reduce gender bias in embeddings while preserving the its useful properties such as the ability to cluster related concepts and to solve analogy tasks. The resulting embeddings can be used in applications without amplifying gender bias.

sample_claims.text: The first three principal components of the sensor network readings account for 90 per cent or more of the variance, so a three-dimensional summary does not discard a material part of the data's structure.
Once the clinical measurements are standardised, no single measurement dominates the leading component, so the main pattern of variation in the patient data does not depend on a measurement's units.

The leading component of the portfolio's risk indicators loads on a recognisable group of related measures, so the main source of variation in the indicators can be named and discussed with the risk committee.
The training images' leading principal components have been inspected and are not dominated by capture artefacts such as lighting or sensor noise.

techniques.name: Prototype and Criticism Models
techniques.description: Prototype and criticism methods summarise a dataset with a small set of real examples. Prototypes are instances chosen to represent the bulk of the data, so that together they match its overall distribution as closely as possible. Criticisms are the instances the prototypes represent worst, which shows what the summary leaves out. In a set of customer transactions, prototypes might be the usual buying patterns and criticisms might be bulk buyers or one-off high-value customers. A reviewer can read a few dozen examples instead of the whole dataset, but the method describes the data only, so how a model performs on the unusual cases needs a separate check.

example_use_cases.description: A radiology team summarises a medical imaging dataset with prototypes and criticisms. The prototypes show the typical scans that dominate the data, and the criticisms show rare presentations the data covers thinly. The team uses the criticisms to choose cases for a separate check of how accurate the model is on rare presentations.

A credit risk team summarises its borrower records with prototypes (typical low-risk profiles) and criticisms (unusual but legitimate patterns, such as irregular self-employed income). It passes the criticism cases to a separate accuracy check, to see whether the scoring model handles them as well as typical borrowers.

An engineer preparing a visual inspection model for a production line computes prototypes and criticisms for each defect class on the model's image embeddings. The criticisms show unusual captures, such as odd lighting or partial views, which the team adds to the test set so the model is checked on them.

limitations.description: Which examples are chosen depends on the similarity measure and its settings, so different reasonable choices give different prototypes and criticisms. The original paper lists the effect of the kernel choice as future work, so there is no settled guidance.
The method needs a similarity score between every pair of examples, so memory and time grow with the square of the dataset size. Large datasets may need to be sampled before the method is run.
The user sets the number of prototypes and criticisms. Too few leaves large parts of the data unrepresented, and too many defeats the purpose of a summary short enough for a person to read.

It describes the data, not the model. Criticisms are the examples the prototypes represent worst, which is not the same as the examples the model gets wrong, so a separate evaluation is needed to learn how the model performs on them.

The original evidence that criticisms help people understand a dataset is a pilot study with four participants. Those who saw prototypes and criticisms were more accurate but slower than those who saw prototypes alone, so the benefit for a given audience is untested.

resources.title: MMD-Critic (BeenKim/MMD-Critic)
Examples are not Enough, Learn to Criticize! Criticism for Interpretability
resources.abstract: Example-based explanations are widely used in the effort to improve the interpretability of highly complex distributions. However, prototypes alone are rarely sufficient to represent the gist of the complexity. In order for users to construct better mental models and understand complex data distributions, we also need criticism to explain what are not captured by prototypes. Motivated by the Bayesian model criticism framework, we develop MMD-critic which efficiently learns prototypes and criticism, designed to aid human interpretability. A human subject pilot study shows that the MMD-critic selects prototypes and criticism that are useful to facilitate human understanding and reasoning. We also evaluate the prototypes selected by MMD-critic via a nearest prototype classifier, showing competitive performance compared to baselines.

resources.title: Prototype selection for interpretable classification
resources.abstract: Prototype methods seek a minimal subset of samples that can serve as a distillation or condensed view of a data set. As the size of modern data sets grows, being able to present a domain specialist with a short list of "representative" samples chosen from the data set is of increasing interpretative value. While much recent statistical research has been focused on producing sparse-in-the-variables methods, this paper aims at achieving sparsity in the samples. We discuss a method for selecting prototypes in the classification setting (in which the samples fall into known discrete categories). Our method of focus is derived from three basic properties that we believe a good prototype set should satisfy. This intuition is translated into a set cover optimization problem, which we solve approximately using standard approaches. While prototype selection is usually viewed as purely a means toward building an efficient classifier, in this paper we emphasize the inherent value of having a set of prototypical elements. That said, by using the nearest-neighbor rule on the set of prototypes, we can of course discuss our method as a classifier as well.

sample_claims.text: The training scans have been summarised by a reviewed set of prototypes and criticisms, and radiologists have confirmed that the criticisms are genuine rare presentations and not artefacts or mislabelled cases.

Every borrower profile flagged as a criticism has been reviewed by credit risk staff and either documented as legitimate or corrected, so the scoring model's evaluation can include atypical applicants.
The monitoring system's training data covers the common measurement conditions shown by its prototypes, and the unusual conditions shown by its criticisms are reflected in the test set.
A short, reviewable summary of the training data (the prototypes) represents its typical contents, and what the summary leaves out (the criticisms) has been listed alongside it.

techniques.name: GAN-Based Tabular Synthetic Data
techniques.description: GAN-based tabular synthetic data generation trains a generative model on a real table, then samples new rows from it to produce a synthetic table that can be shared or used in place of the original. In CTGAN (Conditional Tabular GAN), a generator network learns to produce rows and a discriminator network learns to tell them from real ones. CTGAN suits tables through mode-specific normalisation, which treats each numeric column as a mixture of clusters, and through training-by-sampling, which shows rare categories to the model often enough for it to learn them. TVAE is a related model built on a variational autoencoder, another kind of generative network, rather than a GAN. The synthetic table aims to preserve the original's column distributions and correlations, and its rows are generated rather than copied, but this is not a privacy guarantee, because a generator can memorise and reproduce training rows.

example_use_cases.description: Generating synthetic patient records from hospital databases using CTGAN to enable multi-institution collaborative research on treatment outcomes without sharing identifiable health data across organisational boundaries.

A bank's analytics team generates a synthetic copy of its customer transactions with CTGAN and gives it to an external vendor building a spending-insights dashboard. Before release, the team checks the table for rows that closely match real customers and decides whether it is safe to hand over.

A government statistics office produces a CTGAN synthetic version of a restricted household survey so researchers can develop and test analysis code before applying for access to the real data. The office uses it to decide what can be released openly and what stays in a secure facility.

limitations.description: Training instability inherent to GAN architectures (mode collapse, vanishing gradients) can result in synthetic data that fails to capture the full diversity of the original distribution, particularly for rare categories or tail distributions.

There is no reliable rule for setting CTGAN's hyperparameters, such as epochs, batch size and learning rates, so users must experiment and watch whether the generator and discriminator losses converge. Training time grows with the number of epochs and can be shortened with a GPU.

Privacy guarantees are not inherent. Without additional mechanisms such as differential privacy, GAN-generated data may leak information about training records through memorisation or membership inference attacks.

CTGAN samples each row independently from fully connected networks, so it does not preserve row order, time dependencies or links between tables, and columns with many categories are harder to learn because each value is one-hot encoded.

The synthetic table can only reproduce what the training table contains: biases, gaps and thinly covered subgroups carry over or are lost, and models trained on synthetic rows are normally no better than models trained on the real table they imitate. Fidelity has to be tested separately against real data before the table is used.

resources.title: Modeling Tabular data using Conditional GAN
resources.abstract: Modeling the probability distribution of rows in tabular data and generating realistic synthetic data is a non-trivial task. Tabular data usually contains a mix of discrete and continuous columns. Continuous columns may have multiple modes whereas discrete columns are sometimes imbalanced making the modeling difficult. Existing statistical and deep neural network models fail to properly model this type of data. We design TGAN, which uses a conditional generative adversarial network to address these challenges. To aid in a fair and thorough comparison, we design a benchmark with 7 simulated and 8 real datasets and several Bayesian network baselines. TGAN outperforms Bayesian methods on most of the real datasets whereas other deep learning methods could not.

A Review of Tabular Data Synthesis Using GANs on an IDS Dataset
resources.abstract: Recent technological innovations along with the vast amount of available data worldwide have led to the rise of cyberattacks against network systems. Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) play a crucial role as a defense mechanism in networks against adversarial attackers. Machine Learning methods provide various cybersecurity tools. However, these methods require plenty of data to be trained efficiently, which may be hard to collect or to use due to privacy reasons. One of the most notable Machine Learning tools is the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), and it has great potential for tabular data synthesis. In this work, we start by briefly presenting the most popular GAN architectures, VanillaGAN, WGAN, and WGAN-GP. Focusing on tabular data generation, CTGAN, CopulaGAN, and TableGAN models are used for the creation of synthetic IDS data. Specifically, the models are trained and evaluated on an NSL-KDD dataset, considering the limitations and requirements that this procedure needs. Finally, based on certain quantitative and qualitative methods, we argue and evaluate the most prominent GANs for tabular network data synthesis.

sample_claims.text: The patient table shared with partner institutions consists only of model-generated rows, so no original patient record leaves the hospital's controlled environment
The external vendor built and tested its dashboard on a synthetic copy of the transaction table, so no real customer row was disclosed outside the bank
Every row in the published survey file was generated by a model trained on the restricted data, not copied from a respondent's record

techniques.name: Fairness GAN
techniques.description: Fairness GAN is a pre-processing method that generates a synthetic training dataset in which decisions no longer track a protected attribute such as gender or skin tone. A generative adversarial network (GAN) is a pair of networks trained against each other, one producing fake examples and one trying to tell them from real ones. Here the generator is conditioned on the protected attribute and produces both an example and its decision label, such as hired or rejected (images in the original work, table rows in Xu et al.'s separate FairGAN). An extra network tries to predict the protected attribute from the generated output, and the generator is rewarded for defeating it, so favourable decisions become more similar across groups. The user can aim for demographic parity, meaning equal rates of favourable decisions, or for equality of opportunity, which applies the constraint only to favourable decisions.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment technology team holds interview-video stills labelled with past shortlisting decisions that favoured one gender. It trains a Fairness GAN to generate a synthetic image set whose shortlisting labels are similar for women and men, trains the screening model on that set, and compares shortlisting rates by gender on held-out real images before deployment.

A lender's data science team has ten years of loan decisions in which women were approved less often than men on similar incomes. It trains a tabular FairGAN-style generator to produce a synthetic dataset, confirms that the gap in approval rates in the synthetic data is close to zero, and trains its scoring model on that data, testing accuracy and approval rates on real held-out applications.

limitations.description: GAN training is unstable and the fairness loss adds a further pull on the generator. The original authors used spectral normalisation, softened outcome values and added noise to keep training stable, and results still varied across datasets. Expect tuning effort and repeated runs.

Fairness and accuracy trade off, and the gain is uneven. In the original experiments a classifier trained on debiased CelebA data went from about 20 to about 29 per cent error. Demographic parity improved on three of four datasets but not on Quick, Draw!, and the demographic-parity version made equality of opportunity worse on the soccer data.

It needs a lot of data. The authors had only 1,501 labelled soccer images, so they borrowed more than 200,000 unlabelled CelebA faces to help the generator, which is possible only when a large related set exists.

The original method covers a narrow setting: image inputs, one binary protected attribute and a binary outcome, with demographic parity or equality of opportunity but not equalised odds. Continuous protected attributes and non-image data are left as future work, and tabular versions such as FairGAN are separate methods with their own evidence.

Fairness is judged by training a classifier on the synthetic data and testing it on real data, and image quality is judged mainly by inspecting average faces. The authors report that debiasing visibly changes images in stereotyped ways, such as male faces taking on features coded as feminine, so the synthetic data need checking for distortions that the classifier test would miss.

resources.title: TabFairGAN
Fairness GAN
resources.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Fairness GAN, an approach for generating a dataset that is plausibly similar to a given multimedia dataset, but is more fair with respect to protected attributes in allocative decision making. We propose a novel auxiliary classifier GAN that strives for demographic parity or equality of opportunity and show empirical results on several datasets, including the CelebFaces Attributes (CelebA) dataset, the Quick, Draw!\ dataset, and a dataset of soccer player images and the offenses they were called for. The proposed formulation is well-suited to absorbing unlabeled data; we leverage this to augment the soccer dataset with the much larger CelebA dataset. The methodology tends to improve demographic parity and equality of opportunity while generating plausible images.

resources.title: FairGAN: Fairness-aware Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Fairness-aware learning is increasingly important in data mining. Discrimination prevention aims to prevent discrimination in the training data before it is used to conduct predictive analysis. In this paper, we focus on fair data generation that ensures the generated data is discrimination free. Inspired by generative adversarial networks (GAN), we present fairness-aware generative adversarial networks, called FairGAN, which are able to learn a generator producing fair data and also preserving good data utility. Compared with the naive fair data generation models, FairGAN further ensures the classifiers which are trained on generated data can achieve fair classification on real data. Experiments on a real dataset show the effectiveness of FairGAN.

resources.title: Bt-GAN: Generating Fair Synthetic Healthdata via Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Synthetic data generation offers a promising solution to enhance the usefulness of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) by generating realistic de-identified data. However, the existing literature primarily focuses on the quality of synthetic health data, neglecting the crucial aspect of fairness in downstream predictions. Consequently, models trained on synthetic EHR have faced criticism for producing biased outcomes in target tasks. These biases can arise from either spurious correlations between features or the failure of models to accurately represent sub-groups. To address these concerns, we present Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks (Bt-GAN), a GAN-based synthetic data generator specifically designed for the healthcare domain. In order to tackle spurious correlations (i), we propose an information-constrained Data Generation Process (DGP) that enables the generator to learn a fair deterministic transformation based on a well-defined notion of algorithmic fairness. To overcome the challenge of capturing exact sub-group representations (ii), we incentivize the generator to preserve sub-group densities through score-based weighted sampling. This approach compels the generator to learn from underrepresented regions of the data manifold. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-III) database. Our results demonstrate that Bt-GAN achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while significantly improving fairness and minimizing bias amplification. Furthermore, we perform an in-depth explainability analysis to provide additional evidence supporting the validity of our study. In conclusion, our research introduces a novel and professional approach to addressing the limitations of synthetic data generation in the healthcare domain. By incorporating fairness considerations and leveraging advanced techniques such as GANs, we pave the way for more reliable and unbiased predictions in healthcare applications.

resources.title: FairFinGAN: Fairness-Aware Synthetic Financial Data Generation
resources.abstract: Financial datasets often suffer from bias that can lead to unfair decision-making in automated systems. In this work, we propose FairFinGAN, a WGAN-based framework designed to generate synthetic financial data while mitigating bias with respect to the protected attribute. Our approach incorporates fairness constraints directly into the training process through a classifier, ensuring that the synthetic data is both fair and preserves utility for downstream predictive tasks. We evaluate our proposed model on five real-world financial datasets and compare it with existing GAN-based data generation methods. Experimental results show that our approach achieves superior fairness metrics without significant loss in data utility, demonstrating its potential as a tool for bias-aware data generation in financial applications.

sample_claims.text: In the synthetic training set generated for the screening model, the rate of favourable shortlisting decisions for women and men differs by less than the tolerance set in the project's fairness requirement.
A credit scoring model trained on the synthetic loan data shows a smaller gap in approval rates between women and men, on held-out real applications, than a model trained on the original data.
The synthetic data remain close enough to the original for the model's purpose: the accuracy cost of training on them, compared with the original data, was measured and judged acceptable.
